apex export -applicationid &APP_ID -split -skipExportDate -expOriginalIds -expSupportingObjects N
```

`validate.sql` guards identity, expected target revision, live fingerprints, state, component compatibility and the upgrade path before the first command below. The deployment controller repeats these checks under exclusive ownership before installation; validation alone does not reserve the target. `install.sql` guards identity, runs the second, sets the explicit APEX installation context, imports the split metadata and applies nonsecret target settings:

```text
lb validate -changelog-file db/changelog.xml
lb update -changelog-file db/changelog.xml
```

Options derive from the [APEX 24.2 export reference](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/apex/24.2/aeadm/exporting-one-or-more-applications.html) and [SQLcl 25.3 Liquibase reference](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/sql-developer-command-line/25.3/sqcug/liquibase.html). Prove shell exit behavior for SQL, Liquibase and APEX failures with negative cases; merely printing an error is insufficient.

## Required evidence, not tests implemented in I.1

**SM-1:** Expected target/version/application identity and HTTP route succeed; wrong schema/workspace/application mapping is rejected without writes.

**SM-2:** A reviewed Foundation/Hello/World version triple and supported upgrade path are accepted. An incompatible Hello/World pair, unsupported Foundation version, unexpectedly missing metadata and a mismatch between APEX labels and registry are rejected before deployment writes. Preserve the observed installed set on rejection. Do not infer compatibility from matching major versions alone.

**UT-1:** Seed composition is exactly `Hello World`; prefixes, Unicode and 100-character boundary entries work; empty, oversized and inactive selections fail. **UT-2:** Default ownership/deactivation rules and atomic history insertion hold; configuration changes leave earlier snapshots unchanged.

**IT-1:** Export twice without edits and inspect differences. Validate the current PR candidate in a disposable area; after merge build one accepted-revision archive, qualify those exact bytes for clean reconstruction and the declared additive upgrade, then promote them to user_acceptance_test. Record unchanged archive hash, accepted commit, integration_test/deployment receipts, target configuration identity and observed greeting. Reject stale PR evidence, changed bytes, missing integration_test and unsupported starting versions. Verify disposable reset cannot touch user_acceptance_test history. **IT-2:** Upgrade with an additive database change and a Hello or World change; all 20 prior sentinel history rows retain their complete values. Repeat the archive: migrations/seeds do not duplicate, user_acceptance_test settings remain correct, and DEV data is unchanged. **IT-3:** A failing precheck blocks deployment; a separate failure after committed additive DDL stops subsequent steps. Inspect live partial definitions/version records and authorize a recovery linked to the failed attempt and current generation. Inject an intervening unexplained change and reject recovery until reviewed reconciliation. Qualify the selected new repair archive against the inspected partial state, recheck that starting state under ownership, repair and prove history preservation. Separately establish when unchanged bytes can safely resume. Incomplete observation/unsupported recovery stays blocked; logs alone do not prove what committed. A coordinated upgrade cannot report success with mixed versions. **IT-4:** From the reviewed greenfield seed and bootstrapped control authority, verify the explicit assembly manifest: Foundation-only component checks succeed and release A's reservation while root maintenance blocks ordinary/incomplete dependent behavior; deliberately absent Hello/World are recorded without fake versions. Allow only the declared subsequent assembly stages. Require the complete approved triple for the first operational user_acceptance_test release. The same missing metadata on a previously complete target is rejected. Show Foundation, Hello and World labels, compare them with artifact metadata and installed records, and verify accepted/rejected complete version sets. These are future cases, not tests implemented in I.1.

Automated browser checks sign in, edit each component independently, submit a greeting, reject invalid values, display escaped markup, refresh history and check pagination with 21 rows. SQL and HTTP 200 cannot substitute for that evidence. Manual walkthroughs supplement these automated checks. E.1 covers its accepted thin slice; full-page behavior remains a release gate if deferred from the prototype.

All fixtures are synthetic and confined to dedicated lab targets. Never discard retained history, touch unrelated resources or log secrets; scope teardown to the owned disposable experiment instance. Use local services for execution after tools are provisioned. Record prerequisite failures separately from product failures. Before activating E.1, obtain Product Owner acceptance of this command contract; before claiming tests pass, implement and actually execute them.

## Collaboration evidence proposed after use-case refinement

**IT-5 — Core multi-developer journey:** A starts from the reviewed greenfield seed (or the separately verified UC-12 adoption path), reserves and delivers Foundation through a task branch/PR, passes component-specific assembly checks and releases ownership while the root remains maintenance. Foundation must reconstruct without Hello/World-owned objects. No completed Hello/World application is supplied to bypass their authoring work. From its accepted baseline, B and C reserve and develop Hello and World on separate task branches/targets. The two different-component reservations must coexist. Capture their actual APEX definitions through SQLcl into the appropriate checkout; verify canonical identity/path handling, deletion reconciliation and an unchanged second capture. Reject wrong source mappings or unsafe overwrites of uncommitted work. Merge, import the combined SQL into the validation target and show both intended changes, correct component versions and retained history. Record which state was private/shared. B/C each add a component-owned page/navigation entry so both exports touch shared bookkeeping; retain both additions. After B's acceptance, C incorporates B's accepted revision without treating inherited Hello changes as new C-authored edits. Preserve provenance and revalidate the candidate. The complete accepted application deploys under target ownership without reacquiring authoring reservations for completed/unchanged components.

**IT-6 — Scope enforcement and exceptional reconciliation:** Attempt to capture or integrate a change outside semantic ownership and reject it, including an unauthorized change to shared composition/security/controller behavior. Allow only bounded validated generated-file reconciliation. Discover additional task scope, preserve work, atomically request the complete expanded set and return a conflict if unavailable; verify no partial acquisition or indefinite hold-and-wait. Revalidate the base before resuming. In an explicitly controlled out-of-tool/break-glass variation, introduce same-page/shared version metadata conflicts, then require reviewed reconciliation and renewed import/behavior checks. This variation does not permit two managed tasks to own Hello concurrently. Exercise a page deletion and colliding/ordered database changes. Reject missing dependencies, duplicate page/component identities and stale exports rather than silently dropping work. Use native Working Copy repair only as a break-glass variation, returning the change through reconciliation/PR. Its replacement semantics do not prove Git merge behavior or schema isolation.

E.1 must refine and validate a feasible task-area layout within the selected single-host proof and validate export identity stability before this experiment. These are future case specifications only. No task branches, developer schemas, APEX copies or executable tests were created in I.1.

For the PR flow, IT-5/6 must validate the combined task/target-branch candidate before merge. A changed PR or integration baseline invalidates an earlier result until the updated candidate passes. A failed foundation/compatibility or APEX integration gate blocks merge; CD uses the accepted merged revision. These are pipeline acceptance requirements, not a workflow implemented in I.1.

## Drift, concurrency and state evidence proposed for E.1

**SM-3:** A stale expected generation or changed live APEX fingerprint blocks installation without changing the running target to failed. Missing/mismatched fingerprint profiles or baseline metadata also block an existing-target deploy. Only explicitly approved first provisioning may start without an installed base.

**IT-7 — Drift and break-glass reconciliation:** Establish a successful baseline; recompute its fingerprint without edits and obtain the same result. Change a page in App Builder without changing its version; detect drift and preserve the changed source before any deployment overwrite. Check page deletion/shared metadata coverage and a separate manual schema change. Reconcile a retained emergency fix through a reviewed branch and controlled deployment. Record exact export options and any target-configuration differences. Do not treat an old artifact checksum or migration ledger alone as the live-content check.

**IT-8 — Concurrent deployment:** Two attempts expect the same target revision. Only the owner passing a fresh guarded check may mutate it; the other is rejected or rechecks and rejects the advanced generation. Cover the full application-import scope and dependency versions. Demonstrate how emergency editing is excluded from the check/write interval; our own mutex does not lock App Builder itself. Prove ownership persists across DDL commits, SQLcl subprocesses and connection failure; after restart inspect durable authority/attempt records before recovery. A transaction row lock released by a commit is insufficient.

**IT-9 — State inheritance and recovery:** An untagged Hello page inherits Hello maintenance. An explicitly ready child cannot bypass a blocked ancestor; a failed Foundation blocks dependent actions. Exercise direct URLs, form submits and existing sessions, not merely hidden navigation. Prove maintenance → ready requires all checks, mutation failure remains blocked with a reason, and an interrupted controller cannot silently restore readiness. Reject invalid/missing root state and preserve target state across imports. Verify controlled diagnostics remain usable. After preliminary installation/integrity checks, a dedicated deployment-scoped verifier must exercise the real greeting/history path while ordinary direct submissions and existing sessions remain blocked. Bypass only the active deployment-maintenance restriction; failed/unknown dependencies and normal authorization still block, and negative state tests must observe them. Cover draining/fencing active mutations, no unrestricted import interval, stale verifier permission and interruption. Revoke permission and reconcile final availability/configuration/fingerprint evidence before publishing readiness. Identify verifier-created synthetic rows without changing retained history. Demonstrate authorized failed → maintenance → ready repair with history retained and consistent state/version/fingerprint receipts.

All cases above are specifications only. No SQL, test harness, drift collector, state registry or deployment lock has been implemented or exercised in I.1.


## Initial adoption and complete developer journey

**IT-10 — Bootstrap the golden source (UC-12):** Capture an identified source application and its required database/static dependencies without committing secrets or runtime business data. Record versions/profile/provenance, reconstruct the candidate Git revision in a controlled target and compare required definitions/behavior before accepting the baseline. Missing dependencies, an inconsistent capture, a populated unverified target or unsafe repository overwrite must block adoption. Prove that subsequent release packaging uses the accepted Git revision, not a fresh developer export.

**IT-11 — Developer onboarding and complete cycle (UC-8/9/10/7/4/11):** Start with a documented workstation/access state, verify supported software and permissions, obtain a private development area on the selected single host, and associate it with a task branch/base. Edit a focused page, capture/review/commit, submit and revise a PR, validate/merge, deploy, verify behavior/version/history/receipts, then refresh safely for the next task. Record the environment variant actually tested; do not claim both variants passed from one run. Missing permissions/tooling and uncaptured work must produce actionable blockers rather than silent data loss.

IT-10/11 are future evidence requirements, not implemented or executed tests. The existing smoke/unit/integration command contract remains proposed; Elaboration refines the bounded prototype cases before construction.


**IT-12 — Core early same-component rejection:** After the A/B/C component delivery cycle, synchronize B and C to request Hello in UC-9 from the same accepted base. Exactly one atomic reservation succeeds; the other returns a conflict identifying the owner/task before creating its managed branch, provisioning its task area or permitting editing. Assert no code/version/runtime-state change from the rejected request. Repeat with the other developer winning. Show that reservations of Hello and World can coexist and that reserving Hello prevents a competing task even on another Hello page. After verified completion or safe cancellation, the loser must obtain fresh ownership against the new accepted baseline. Validate stale-token rejection after authorized reassignment and atomic all-or-none acquisition for a change spanning multiple components.

IT-5 and IT-12 are required proof-of-concept evidence for the multi-developer design. IT-8 separately covers the target deployment race; it cannot substitute for early task rejection. These specifications have not been implemented or executed in I.1.

## Automation interface validation

SRS FR-13 is a foundation requirement. Validate architecture inventory AI-1–10 during Elaboration, at the depth of each approved experiment. For each entry record the exact tool/server versions, executable command or API sequence, target and required grants, inputs/outputs, successful unattended run, relevant rejection/failure case, exit status and redacted evidence. Mark each entry validated, failed or not yet exercised; a proposed API or successful administrator-only run does not establish routine CI readiness. This evidence requirement is part of selecting the tools, not a separate product feature.

Use the established cases rather than duplicating them: SM-1/IT-11 for connection/provisioning; IT-1/5/10 for capture/import; IT-2/3 for migrations; SM-3/IT-7 for drift; IT-8/9/12 and SM-2 for release/state/version/ownership controls; UT-1/2 and automated browser assertions for application behavior; IT-5/11 and scoped lifecycle experiments for orchestration/infrastructure. Recovery after an injected failure must also execute through the supported command/API path after the required human decision. Record any uncovered operation as an architectural gap and refine the plan before claiming the automation requirement satisfied. No interface validation or browser test implementation is claimed in I.1.

## Elaboration order and architecture exit

Refine PBI-011 into bounded children at E.1 setup/design, with approval before construction. First prove control bootstrap, topology/permissions and minimal atomic reservation/reassignment with concurrent clients; ownership feasibility must not wait until the full system exists. Then prove initial assembly, capture/identity and combined reconstruction, immutable archive integration_test, guarded delivery/verification/repair, and the complete A/B/C cycle including the Hello race. Reuse the cases above rather than creating a feature per mechanism.

Lifecycle Architecture requires evidence for these core controls under the selected topology and supported clean/additive-upgrade/repair paths. Complete page layouts, exhaustive input combinations and additional workstation variants may remain for Construction. If critical feasibility remains open, propose further Elaboration instead of declaring the architecture stable. This is an experiment/exit recommendation, not an E.1 activation or child-PBI assignment.

### Bounded initial-release subcase

Run `bash tests/run.sh --integration --new-only tests/manifests/initial_release.manifest` after initial Q/user_acceptance_test publication and explicit post-delivery sentinel preparation. This read-only delivery repeat check compares all retained history/configuration fields, requires matching successful archive receipts and live APEX fingerprints, and checks the fixture remains repeatable. It verifies the existing initial result; it does not perform fresh reconstruction. Full IT-1 upgrade/repeat-import and IT-2 patch criteria remain pending. Browser verification is separate, as documented in the E.1 test evidence.

### Selected Hello patch and protection increment

Run `bash tests/run.sh --integration --new-only tests/manifests/patch_protections.manifest` for IT-2, SM-2 and the focused IT-7 page-drift slice after both patch integration_tests and user_acceptance_test publication. IT-2 verifies identical-byte receipts for fresh/initial-upgrade starts, live fingerprints and field-level preservation of the retained 21-row baselines; its correction fixture rolls back. SM-2 exercises the incompatible proposal gate with before/after target/control comparisons. IT-7 checks real Oracle error propagation versus stored diagnostic text, injects the separately authored native page fixture, rejects drift and explicitly restores the original fingerprint while preserving data.

The fixture sequence replaces user_acceptance_test APEX definitions and may require runtime re-login; stop other user_acceptance_test authoring/deployment first. It does not rebuild/reset retained user_acceptance_test or install business seed. The initial-release manifest applies only while both live targets still contain that initial release; it is historical after upgrading. The full IT-1 candidate/reconstruction gate and broader concurrency, schema drift, maintenance/verifier fencing and repair acceptance remain open; passing the selected manifest is not a full integration/sprint-completion claim.

### Fresh walkthrough lifecycle

Run `bash tests/run.sh --unit --new-only tests/manifests/walkthrough_lifecycle.manifest` for the cleanup ownership boundary: allow only the known lab inventory; reject unrelated consumers of named volumes/network/secret and unexpected mounts/images before mutation. These local policy tests do not substitute for Oracle isolation or concurrency tests. After A–H, run `bash tests/run.sh --integration --new-only tests/manifests/walkthrough_lifecycle.manifest` for the registered IT-2 result/preservation assertions against this fresh cycle; it does not rerun cleanup.

The same focused unit manifest also tests infrastructure exclusion, control-only setup, single-area provisioning/reset and developer password/profile scope. These mocks test responsibility boundaries, not Oracle concurrency.

The destructive fresh-start experiment is a separate explicit operator sequence in [deploy.md](deploy.md#fresh-walkthrough-infrastructure-sequence): prerequisites, named host preparation, complete lab cleanup and fresh database/APEX/ORDS installation. It must first prove **zero project schemas/workspaces immediately after infrastructure installation**. Then explicitly initialize project control, provision each named area, configure each developer with only their assigned password, and run readiness/isolation checks before A–H. Provisioning and private developer setup must not be hidden in infrastructure installation. It is not part of ordinary regression and must never be invoked as a hidden fixture reset. The A–H rehearsal then executes reviewed source installation, new integration_test/promotion receipts, both patch starts, this-cycle field preservation and selected rejections/restoration. CLI runtime examples are explicitly synthetic verification; browser checkpoints remain separate in live mode. Archives/credentials remain on the host; no prior business history is restored. Broader concurrency/maintenance/recovery criteria remain unchanged.

## C browser-verification retry control

Run `bash tests/run.sh --unit --new-only tests/manifests/development_verification.manifest` for the selected C checkpoint loop: retry a missing required snapshot, exit on q, and stop on unexpected SQL failure. These control-flow tests stub Oracle/browser boundaries. The exact saved Hello World by VERIFIER remains required; other text may be valid business data but does not satisfy that walkthrough fixture. See [C verification steps](../progress/E.1/cicd-walkthrough.md#c-deliver-world-and-complete-the-assembly) and [observed results](../progress/E.1/sprint_E.1_tests.md).

## Release browser-verification retry and bounded UAT resume

The same verification manifest now also checks D/E/F's missing-fixture retry, q and unexpected SQL failure paths. E alone adds a restricted initial 1.0.0 continuation after ORA-20619: validate the same archive/epoch/owner and root/native checkpoint, rerun archived integrity and rollback unit checks, repeat the browser assertion and then use archived publication. No migration/import/reset or new attempt is allowed. See [E continuation](../progress/E.1/cicd-walkthrough.md#resume-e-at-its-restricted-verification-checkpoint) and [operator guidance](../progress/E.1/user_manual.md#resume-initial-uat-verification).

## Post-publication upgrade-example preparation

E's announced UAT history fixture must work when active Hello/World entries were explicitly selected in the UI and a default remains unset. It selects active entries explicitly, preserves configuration and old history, and appends only the missing snapshots to reach twenty. A bounded post-publication continuation requires the same ready initial archive/live fingerprint and compares an existing preservation baseline rather than replacing it. See [E continuation](../progress/E.1/cicd-walkthrough.md#resume-e-after-publication-prepare-upgrade-examples) and [operator guidance](../progress/E.1/user_manual.md#resume-uat-upgrade-example-preparation). This is test-data preparation, not failed-deployment repair.

## Manual Page Designer drift demonstration

[H.1](../progress/E.1/cicd-walkthrough.md#h1-change-a-page-in-app-builder) adds an operator-executed variation of the selected IT-7/PBI-011.7 page-drift check, with evidence under PBI-012 and UC-5/FR-10. Start from a matching published patch; save a single reversible page-title edit in E1_UAT without changing versions; require the actual preflight's specific drift rejection and unchanged snapshots. Restore the exact property and require the original published fingerprint. Temporary workspace developer access is removed after the demonstration. [Operator guidance](../progress/E.1/user_manual.md#manual-page-designer-drift-demonstration) links the same procedure. This variation is documented for manual execution; no new browser execution is claimed. Schema drift, general reconciliation and concurrency remain outside this demonstration.

## Drift check outcomes

The [three demonstrations](../progress/E.1/cicd-walkthrough.md#h-reject-deployment-over-unexpected-live-change) use the same operator drift command on unchanged content, a manual Page Designer edit and a scripted fixture edit. The checker classifies only a specific successful preflight as NO DRIFT and only a specific nonzero fingerprint rejection as DETECTED DRIFT; arbitrary errors cannot pass. Both recognized outcomes require unchanged before/after target/control snapshots. Default checker success means the inspection/protection assertion passed; it does not authorize deployment over drift. Optional --expect-clean/--expect-drift asserts an expected phase for automated testing. H requires clean before injection/restoration completion and drift after injection. [The operator manual](../progress/E.1/user_manual.md#one-drift-check-three-demonstrations) describes these same outcomes.

Run `bash tests/run.sh --unit --new-only tests/manifests/protection_outcomes.manifest` for clean, drift, unexpected Oracle failure, silent failure, missing expected drift, unexpected baseline drift and compatibility regression cases. These focused tests classify captured controller output; they do not perform browser editing or deployment.

## Read-only drift source review

The [H.1 review/decision/restoration steps](../progress/E.1/cicd-walkthrough.md#h1-change-a-page-in-app-builder) and [operator explanation](../progress/E.1/user_manual.md#inspect-manual-drift-before-deciding-restoration) separate source comparison from the user's decision to restore edited properties. cicd-drift-diff.py requires the exact successful patch/source/configuration receipt, captures native APEX source and checks stable fingerprint/receipt across capture. It prints page attribute differences and preserves both source trees, review.diff and raw.diff. Only target offset lines and generated Manifest comments are removed in the shorter comparison; behavior, unknown differences and deployment metadata remain visible. No source import, data mutation, Git update or baseline adoption occurs.

Run `bash tests/run.sh --unit --new-only tests/manifests/drift_review.manifest` for five underlying cases: bounded normalization with complete raw diff, added/deleted source, escaped region names, unrelated receipt rejection and unchanged source. The native manual-drift check reports the current Home title/region changes without restoration. This is APEX source review, not a general SQL semantic diff or failed-deployment recovery tool. Restoration acceptance still requires the original published live fingerprint, not merely a clean text diff.

The operator entry point for that source review is `bash scripts/cicd-protection-check.sh drift --show`. After a recognized drift rejection and unchanged-snapshot checks, it invokes the read-only comparison helper; a clean result reports no unexpected differences to display. Review failures propagate as nonzero without restoration. H.2 uses --expect-drift --show together. The protection-outcome manifest also covers --show with expected outcomes, rejection of compatibility --show and conflicting/duplicate flags.


## Review repair and clean-checkout validation

`bash scripts/cicd-walkthrough-I_repair.sh --rehearse` explicitly executes the selected native BUG-7 failure/observation/repair/negative/repeat experiment in disposable integration. It requires a fresh case, known ready 1.0.1 start and at least twenty baseline rows. It does not replace full IT-3/9 concurrency/unknown-state coverage or browser validation. [Recorded proof](../progress/E.1/tests/recovery_proof_20261018.txt) shows 21 preserved rows/settings and retained failure/success history. [Independent checkout procedure](deploy.md#independent-checkout-rehearsal-while-retaining-the-current-lab) validates clean source/inputs in a separate VM while preserving the retained lab intact; its results must be recorded before claiming that gate passed.

## E.3 implemented pipeline checks

The [E.3 specification](../progress/E.3/sprint_E.3_design.md#test-specification)
retains SM-1/IT-1/IT-2. These parent commands perform fixed **reference-run
regression**, not selected-LAB replay acceptance:

```bash
bash tests/run.sh --smoke --new-only progress/E.3/new_tests.manifest
bash tests/run.sh --integration --new-only progress/E.3/new_tests.manifest
bash tests/run.sh --smoke
```

The recorded historical totals are 1/1, 2/2 and 2/2. SM-1 statically checks the
example workflows, configuration boundary and nine PR classification fixtures.
IT-1/IT-2 hard-code rstyczynski/APEX_CICD_E3 and
progress/E.3/tests/github-environment-journey.json: deployment 41679427616,
qualification 41679432928, tag v1.0.4. They read existing public run metadata and
download retained artifacts into disposable directories; they do not dispatch
workflows, create a clone with a missing file or execute native verification.
A new download is not a new workflow result, and artifacts can expire.

IT-1 checks the recorded PR/tag/archive/changelog identities and reported setup,
preservation and cleanup steps. IT-2 checks the recorded qualification receipt,
positive log and the specific missing-file ERROR/count/path using the shared
assertion. Compatibility with its path-less legacy receipt is allowed only for
the pinned original source/run/path; new-format receipts require the selected
path and controller identity. Historical receipts are never rewritten.

Platform smoke makes a current HTTP probe using the **seed** environment's ORDS
and application variables. It requires permission to read that seed environment;
public source access or LAB ownership is insufficient. It checks a login form,
not LAB_USER authentication or the selected LAB's current state. Parent checks
need gh, Git, jq, Node, curl, shasum and awk; SM-1 also needs actionlint. They
need no local database passwords or private snapshots.

For a new LAB replay, use the operator repository and actual source/release PRs,
generated tag/source SHA, deployment receipt/archive identity and native logs,
separate qualification run if performed, and browser title/history observations.
Passing seed readers cannot substitute for those checks or be required of every
LAB operator. Wider drift/fencing/identity and new-host reproduction remain deferred.

The review's focused offline classifier/receipt regression is separate:

```bash
bash tests/unit/test_missing_changeset.sh
```

It exercises the actual assertions against retained and synthetic diagnostic
fixtures, including unrelated errors, wrong paths, incomplete output, ANSI and
wrapped paths, and new/legacy receipt constraints. It does not connect to Oracle,
dispatch qualification or establish a new native runtime success.


## E.4 qualified experiment boundary

The [accepted E.4 design](../progress/E.4/sprint_E.4_design.md) and
[current evidence](../progress/E.4/sprint_E.4_tests.md) qualify three independent
native author processes, a later announced release branch, separate A/C opt-in and
manager admission, B preservation, and supported central DEV synchronization/repeat.
One Codex operator simulated the roles; no three-human study or production fencing
is claimed. The native checksum changed after exact title restoration because the
only remaining full-source difference was p_version_scn; the Product Owner approved
reviewed counter-only recovery. Status API operations also change fingerprints.
The [manual](../progress/E.4/user_manual.md) owns the bounded operating procedure;
[handover](../progress/E.4/sprint_E.4_handover.md) owns review/acceptance. Broader
product obligations remain unchanged. [PLAN](../PLAN.md) owns assignment and status.


E.4 uses the existing runner with `progress/E.4/new_tests.manifest` for A1/A3 and
`progress/E.4/regression_tests.manifest` for the approved native-pipeline B1 slice.
The grouped integration assertions validate current runtime receipts and read-only
GitHub evidence; they do not replay target writes. The actual native/browser cases,
controlled-restoration correction and exact outcome boundaries are in the linked
test report. Unit tests and broader E.1 runtime regression are not selected here.

# Contractor Agent - Contracting Phase Specialist

**Role**: Establish Agent Cooperation Specification and confirm understanding of project rules.

**Phase**: 1/5 - Contracting

## Do not repeat yourself  

If in current session contracting was already completed - do not execute this phase, as contracting was already executed. Make a note that contracting was already done in previous Sprint. You my add symbolic link to the actual contracting confirmation.

## Responsibilities

1. Review project scope in BACKLOG.md
2. Review implementation plan in PLAN.md
3. Review all rules in `rules/generic` directory
4. Apply rules in `rules/specific` only to technologies explicitly selected for the project
5. Confirm understanding of cooperation rules
6. Document any unclear points or conflicts
7. Summarize understanding and readiness

## Execution

Execute the contracting phase by following these instructions:

### Step 1: Read Foundation Documents

Read the following documents to understand the project:

1. `AGENTS.md` - General instructions for agents
2. `BACKLOG.md` - Project scope and requirements
3. `PLAN.md` - Implementation plan and Sprint organization
4. `progress/` directory - Previously completed work

### Step 2: Review Cooperation Rules

Read and confirm understanding of all rules:

**Generic Rules (technology-agnostic):**
1. `rules/generic/GENERAL_RULES.md` - General cooperation rules
2. `rules/generic/PRODUCT_OWNER_GUIDE.md` - Product Owner workflow
3. `rules/generic/GIT_RULES.md` - Git repository rules

**Technology-Specific Rules (based on project):**
4. `rules/<technology>/` directory - Check for technology-specific development rules
   - For GitHub Actions projects: `rules/github_actions/GitHub_DEV_RULES.md`
   - For Ansible projects: `rules/ansible/` (future)
   - For Terraform projects: `rules/terraform/` (future)

### Step 3: Validate Understanding

For each document reviewed:
- Summarize key points
- Identify any unclear or conflicting requirements
- Note any concerns or potential issues
- Confirm compliance capability

### Step 4: Enumerate Responsibilities

List your responsibilities as an Implementor:
- What you are allowed to edit
- What you must never modify
- How to propose changes
- How to ask questions
- Status tokens and state machines
- Git commit requirements

### Step 5: Document Understanding

Create a contracting summary that includes:

1. **Project Overview**: Brief description of the project goals
2. **Current Sprint**: Identify Sprint(s) in `Progress` status
3. **Key Requirements**: Summary of active Backlog Items
4. **Rule Compliance**: Confirmation of understanding for each rule document
5. **Responsibilities**: Clear enumeration of Implementor role
6. **Constraints**: List of prohibited actions
7. **Communication Protocol**: How to propose changes and ask questions
8. **Open Questions**: Any unclear points requiring clarification

### Step 6: Create Contracting Summary

Once the contract is clear:

- collect statistics about LLM tokens used for this phase to be added the phase summary
- save your contracting summary `progress/sprint_${no}/sprint_${no}_contract.md`

### Step 6: Finalize

**If anything is unclear:**
- Stop here
- List all open questions
- Wait for clarifications from Product Owner
- Do NOT proceed to commit

**If everything is clear:**
- Confirm your readiness to proceed
- State: "Contracting phase complete - ready for Inception"
- Commit the contracting review file following semantic commit conventions

# Test Procedures

Combined procedures for Test Architect (Phase 2) and Test Executor (Phase 4).

---

## Part 1: Test Architect Procedure

**When:** During Phase 2 (Design), after writing the design document.
**Input:** Design document with `### Testing Strategy` section, `Test:` parameter from PLAN.md.
**Output:** Test specifications embedded in design.md, test skeletons in `tests/`, `new_tests.manifest`.

### Step 1: Detect Test Scope

Read the `Test:` field from PLAN.md (or Phase 0 banner):

| Test: Value | Action |
|-------------|--------|
| `smoke` | Create smoke test specs and skeletons in `tests/smoke/` |
| `unit` | Create unit test specs and skeletons in `tests/unit/` |
| `integration` | Create integration test specs and skeletons in `tests/integration/` |
| `none` | Note "no new tests; regression only" — skip to Step 5 |

### Step 2: Write Test Specifications

Append `## Test Specification` section to `sprint_N_design.md`:

```markdown
## Test Specification

Sprint Test Configuration:
- Test: [value from PLAN.md]
- Mode: [value from PLAN.md]

### Smoke Tests (if applicable)

#### SM-1: [Critical Functionality Check]
- **What it verifies:** [most important behavior]
- **Pass criteria:** [expected result]
- **Why smoke:** [why critical for fast gate]
- **Target file:** tests/smoke/test_[name].sh

### Unit Tests (if applicable)

#### UT-1: [Function Under Test]
- **Input:** [defined input]
- **Expected Output:** [exact expected output]
- **Edge Cases:** [boundary conditions]
- **Isolation:** [mocks/stubs needed]
- **Target file:** tests/unit/test_[component].sh

### Integration Tests (if applicable)

#### IT-1: [End-to-End Scenario]
- **Preconditions:** [infrastructure, secrets, tools]
- **Steps:** [ordered sequence]
- **Expected Outcome:** [observable result]
- **Verification:** [how to assert]
- **Target file:** tests/integration/test_[domain].sh

### Traceability

| Backlog Item | Smoke | Unit Tests | Integration Tests |
|--------------|-------|------------|-------------------|
| PBI-N | SM-1 | UT-1, UT-2 | IT-1 |
```

### Step 3: Create Test Skeletons

For each test case, append to the appropriate file in `tests/`:

**Principles:**
- One file per component/domain, NOT per sprint
- New test cases are appended as functions to existing files
- Use `# TODO: implement` markers where code-under-test will be called
- Skeletons must be runnable — they fail (red) before implementation

**Skeleton template:**

```bash
test_UT1_function_name() {
    echo "=== UT-1: [Function Under Test] ==="

    # Setup
    local input="test input"
    local expected="expected output"

    # Execute
    # TODO: implement — call the function under test
    local actual=""

    # Assert
    if [[ "$actual" == "$expected" ]]; then
        echo "PASS: UT-1"
        return 0
    else
        echo "FAIL: UT-1 — expected '$expected', got '$actual'"
        return 1
    fi
}
```

### Step 4: Write New-Tests Manifest

Create `progress/sprint_N/new_tests.manifest`:

```text
# Sprint N new tests — used by tests/run.sh --new-only

# Smoke tests
smoke:test_critical.sh

# Unit tests (specific functions)
unit:test_emit.sh:test_UT1_function_name
unit:test_emit.sh:test_UT2_edge_cases

# Integration tests (specific functions)
integration:test_sli.sh:test_IT1_full_pipeline
```

Format: `suite:script[:function]`
- If no function specified, entire script is new
- Used by `--new-only` flag to run only sprint's new tests

### Step 5: Register in Component Manifest

Add new test entries to appropriate component manifest in `tests/manifests/`:

```text
# tests/manifests/component_emit.manifest
unit:test_emit.sh
integration:test_sli.sh
```

### Step 6: Verify Skeletons Run

```bash
tests/run.sh --unit    # Should report N failures, 0 passes for new tests
tests/run.sh --smoke   # Should pass (smoke tests may just check preconditions)
```

### Step 7: Update PROGRESS_BOARD.md

Set Backlog Item status to `test_specified`.

## Part 2: Test Executor Procedure

**When:** Phase 4 (Quality Gates), after construction is complete.
**Input:** Implementation code, test skeletons filled, `Test:` and `Regression:` parameters.
**Output:** Test logs, `sprint_N_tests.md`, PROGRESS_BOARD updates.

### Gate Execution Order

```
Phase A: New-Code Gates (per Test: parameter)
    A1 Smoke → A2 Unit → A3 Integration

Phase B: Regression Gates (per Regression: parameter, after Phase A passes)
    B1 Smoke → B2 Unit → B3 Integration
```

Each gate must pass before proceeding to the next.

### Mandatory Log Artifacts

**Every gate execution MUST produce a timestamped log file.**

```bash
TS="$(date -u '+%Y%m%d_%H%M%S')"
LOG="progress/sprint_N/test_run_<gate>_${TS}.log"
tests/run.sh --<level> [flags] 2>&1 | tee "$LOG"
echo "Test log: $LOG"
```

Gate names: `A1_smoke`, `A2_unit`, `A3_integration`, `B1_smoke`, `B2_unit`, `B3_integration`

### Phase A: New-Code Gates

Run only new tests from `new_tests.manifest`:

**Gate A1 — Smoke** (if `Test:` includes `smoke`):
```bash
TS="$(date -u '+%Y%m%d_%H%M%S')"
LOG="progress/sprint_N/test_run_A1_smoke_${TS}.log"
tests/run.sh --smoke --new-only progress/sprint_N/new_tests.manifest 2>&1 | tee "$LOG"
```

**Gate A2 — Unit** (if `Test:` includes `unit`):
```bash
TS="$(date -u '+%Y%m%d_%H%M%S')"
LOG="progress/sprint_N/test_run_A2_unit_${TS}.log"
tests/run.sh --unit --new-only progress/sprint_N/new_tests.manifest 2>&1 | tee "$LOG"
```

**Gate A3 — Integration** (if `Test:` includes `integration`):
```bash
TS="$(date -u '+%Y%m%d_%H%M%S')"
LOG="progress/sprint_N/test_run_A3_integration_${TS}.log"
tests/run.sh --integration --new-only progress/sprint_N/new_tests.manifest 2>&1 | tee "$LOG"
```

### Phase B: Regression Gates

Run full suite (or scoped by `Regression scope:`):

**Gate B1 — Smoke Regression** (if `Regression:` includes `smoke`):
```bash
TS="$(date -u '+%Y%m%d_%H%M%S')"
LOG="progress/sprint_N/test_run_B1_smoke_${TS}.log"
tests/run.sh --smoke [--component <scope>] 2>&1 | tee "$LOG"
```

**Gate B2 — Unit Regression** (if `Regression:` includes `unit`):
```bash
TS="$(date -u '+%Y%m%d_%H%M%S')"
LOG="progress/sprint_N/test_run_B2_unit_${TS}.log"
tests/run.sh --unit [--component <scope>] 2>&1 | tee "$LOG"
```

**Gate B3 — Integration Regression** (if `Regression:` includes `integration`):
```bash
TS="$(date -u '+%Y%m%d_%H%M%S')"
LOG="progress/sprint_N/test_run_B3_integration_${TS}.log"
tests/run.sh --integration [--component <scope>] 2>&1 | tee "$LOG"
```

### Retry Policy

| Mode | Retries 1-4 | Retry 5 | Retries 6-10 | After 10 |
|------|-------------|---------|--------------|----------|
| Managed | Auto fix-and-rerun | Human escalation | Continue if approved | Sprint `failed` |
| YOLO | Auto fix-and-rerun | Auto | Auto | Sprint `failed` |

**Human escalation options (retry 5, managed mode):**
1. Continue retrying (grant 5 more attempts)
2. Mark sprint `failed` and stop
3. Reclassify failure (see `test_failure_classification.md`)

### YOLO Mode Thresholds

| Test Level | Required Pass Rate |
|------------|-------------------|
| Smoke | 100% (no exceptions) |
| Unit | 100% (no exceptions) |
| Integration | ≥80% with failures documented |

### On Failure

1. Capture failure details (test name, error, stack trace)
2. Hand failure report to Constructor
3. Constructor fixes the code
4. Test Executor re-runs the failing gate
5. Repeat until pass or retries exhausted

### Output: sprint_N_tests.md

```markdown
# Sprint N — Test Execution Results

## Summary

| Gate | Result | Retries | Pass Rate |
|------|--------|---------|-----------|
| A1 Smoke | PASS | 0 | 100% |
| A2 Unit | PASS | 1 | 100% |
| A3 Integration | PASS | 0 | 100% |
| B2 Unit | PASS | 0 | 100% |
| B3 Integration | PASS | 0 | 100% |

## Artifacts

| Gate | Log File |
|------|----------|
| A1 Smoke | `test_run_A1_smoke_20240115_143022.log` |
| A2 Unit | `test_run_A2_unit_20240115_143045.log` |
| ... | ... |

## Failures (if any)

- **Error:** Expected 'success', got 'error'
- **Fix:** Corrected return value handling in emit.sh:45

```

After each gate:

# Testing Strategy Template

This template is used by the Designer in Phase 2 (Design) to specify the testing approach. The Test Architect uses this section to create test specifications and skeletons.

## Template

Include this section in `sprint_N_design.md`:

```markdown
### Testing Strategy

#### Recommended Sprint Parameters

- **Test:** [smoke, unit, integration — with rationale for each level]
- **Regression:** [smoke, unit, integration — with rationale]
- **Regression scope:** [component name or omit for full suite]

#### Unit Test Targets

For each component modified or created:

| Component | Functions to Test | Key Inputs & Edge Cases | Isolation (Mocks) |
|-----------|-------------------|-------------------------|-------------------|
| `path/to/file.sh` | `function_name` | Valid input, empty input, special chars | Mock external API calls |

#### Integration Test Scenarios

For each end-to-end path affected:

| Scenario | Infrastructure Dependencies | Expected Outcome | Est. Runtime |
|----------|----------------------------|------------------|--------------|
| Full pipeline execution | OCI tenancy, secrets | Event visible in OCI logs | 2-3 min |

#### Smoke Test Candidates

Which tests are critical enough for the fast gate:

| Candidate | Why Critical | Expected Runtime |
|-----------|--------------|------------------|
| Basic emit validation | If this fails, nothing works | < 5 sec |
```

## Field Descriptions

### Test Parameter Values

| Value | When to Use |
|-------|-------------|
| `smoke` | Always include for quick "is it buildable" check |
| `unit` | Pure logic changes, function-level testing |
| `integration` | End-to-end paths, infrastructure interaction |
| `none` | Documentation-only sprints |

### Regression Parameter Values

| Value | When to Use |
|-------|-------------|
| `smoke` | Fastest — just critical paths |
| `unit` | Good balance of speed and safety |
| `integration` | Maximum safety, slowest |
| `none` | Experimental/throwaway sprints only |

### Regression Scope

Optional. Limits regression to a specific component's manifest:

| Scope Value | Manifest File |
|-------------|---------------|
| `router` | `tests/manifests/component_router.manifest` |
| `emit` | `tests/manifests/component_emit.manifest` |
| `oci-setup` | `tests/manifests/component_oci_setup.manifest` |
| `sli-metrics` | `tests/manifests/component_sli_metrics.manifest` |
| `install` | `tests/manifests/component_install.manifest` |

Omit `Regression scope:` to run full suite regression.

# General cooperation rules

## General rules

This file defines cooperation rules for the RUP (Rational Unified Process) implementation. These rules apply to both:

- Legacy single-agent mode: `@rup-cycle.md`
- Modern multi-agent architecture: `@rup-manager.md` and individual agent commands

You act as an Implementor of goals specified by Product Owner in Software Requirements Specification (SRS) document. In the multi-agent architecture, the "Implementor" role is realized through specialized agents:

- **Contractor Agent**: Phase 1 - Contracting (rule review and confirmation)
- **Analyst Agent**: Phase 2 - Inception (requirements analysis)
- **Designer Agent**: Phase 3 - Elaboration (technical design)
- **Constructor Agent**: Phase 4 - Construction (implementation and testing)
- **Documentor Agent**: Phase 5 - Documentation (validation and updates)

The project is divided into Sprints. The execution roadmap lives in `PLAN.md`, which enumerates `Sprints` as sub chapters referring to `Backlog Items` listed in `BACKLOG.md` file.

The Implementor is expected to review the entire `PLAN.md` document with special attention to the current `Sprint`. Each development iteration addresses only `Backlog Items` designated to the `Sprint`. Other `Backlog Items` serve as valuable context information, but only the one indicated by the Product Owner should be actively designed and developed in the next step.

The Implementor concentrates on the requirements stated in the Implementation Plan within `PLAN.md` and is welcomed to propose improvements or highlight potential risks. Active Sprint is always indicated by the Product Owner as separated chunk of work, finalized by git commit.

All the proposed changes are written to `Proposed changes` chapter. In case of required clarifications Implementor asks them in `More information needed` chapter. Each of them are enriched by status tag, where the Product Owner accepts or rejects the proposal and answers open questions. Accepted changes are added to a Backlog. Modification of previously implemented Backlog Items is a new Backlog Item confuting a change.

The produced code is simplistic implementation of specified requirements without any additions.

If you see requirement or any extra feature to add propose it in `Proposed change` chapter. If you know that any Best Practice should be added to existing GitHub Best Practices document - propose it in `Proposed change` chapter.

Product Owner creates general Implementation Plan in `PLAN.md` that is subject for discussion. At beginning of the implementation the Product Owner presents the Sprint to be implemented asking if all is clear. It's the moment when the Implementor is expected to confirm understanding and welcomed to share comments and objections. Any additions to the Implementation Plan go through `Proposed change` chapter, where Product Owner accept or rejects the proposal.

The Implementor is responsible for creating the design in `Design` chapter under separated subchapter directly linked with the Sprint name from `PLAN.md`.  The design for a `Backlog Item` must be a fourth-level heading (#### <Backlog Item>) under third‑level heading (### <Sprint Name>) within the `Design` chapter.

The design must begin with a feasibility analysis of the requirements versus the available GitHub API. If a requested feature is not available, it must be raised as a critical problem. The Product Owner will then decide whether to reject the requirement.

The Design must be approved by a status on top of the chapter, before Implementor starts the actual coding. Design is always supported by references to the documentation.

## Feedback Mechanism

Throughout the process, the Implementor can:

1. **Propose Changes:** Write to `progress/sprint_<id>/sprint_<id>_proposedchanges.md`
2. **Request Clarifications:** Write to `progress/sprint_<id>/sprint_<id>_openquestions.md`
3. Product Owner marks feedback (PROPOSED, ACCEPTED, REJECTED, POSTPONED)
4. Accepted changes move to Implementation Plan via Backlog

## Feedback from the Implementor

Implementation agent is requested to ask for clarifications and propose new features when it's required or appropriate.

Feedback from the Implementor raising proposed changes and requesting clarifications is owned by the Implementor and is stored in `progress/sprint_<id>/sprint_<id>_proposedchanges.md` and `progress/sprint_<id>/sprint_<id>_openquestions.md` files for each Sprint.

The file `progress/sprint_<id>/sprint_<id>_proposedchanges.md` is owned by the Implementor and contains proposed changes to the initial plan. Use subchapter following the Backlog Items's name. The Product Owner, after accepting the feedback, moves proposals to the implementation plan trough Backlog list. You can only append to this chapter. Never edit already existing paragraphs.

Template of the file is following:

```markdown
# Sprint <id> - Feedback

## <Proposal A>
Status: None
```

The file `progress/sprint_<id>/sprint_<id>_openquestions.md` contains clarification requests from the Implementor. Use subchapter following the problem's name. The Product Owner, after accepting the question, answers here. You can append to this chapter. Never edit already existing paragraphs.

Template of the file is following:

```markdown
# Sprint <id> - More information needed

## <Question A>
Status: None
Problem to clarify: None
Answer: None
```

## Execution Modes

The RUP process supports two execution modes configured in `PLAN.md`:

### Mode: managed (Default - Interactive)

**Characteristics:**

- Human-supervised execution
- Agents ask for clarification on ambiguities
- Interactive decision-making at each phase
- Recommended for complex or high-risk sprints

**Behavior:**

- Wait for design approval
- Stop for unclear requirements
- Ask about significant implementation choices
- Confirm before making major decisions

### Mode: YOLO (Autonomous - "You Only Live Once")

**Characteristics:**

- Fully autonomous execution
- Agents make reasonable assumptions for weak problems
- No human interaction required
- All decisions logged in implementation docs
- Recommended for well-understood, low-risk sprints

**Behavior:**

- Auto-approve designs
- Make reasonable assumptions (documented)
- Proceed with partial test success
- Auto-fix simple issues
- Only stop for critical failures

**Decision Logging:**

All YOLO mode decisions are logged in phase documents with:

- What was ambiguous
- What assumption was made
- Rationale for the decision
- Risk assessment

**Audit Trail:**
The Mode field in PLAN.md creates a permanent git record showing which sprints were autonomous vs supervised.

**How to Detect Mode:**
Read the active Sprint section in PLAN.md:

```markdown
## Sprint 20

Status: Progress
Mode: YOLO          ← Autonomous mode active

Backlog Items:
* GH-27. Feature implementation
```

If no Mode field or `Mode: managed` → Interactive mode (default)

### YOLO Mode Speed Rules

When in YOLO mode, optimize for speed as directed in Sprint label `Speed`.

**Speed Levels:**

- `FAST`: minimal docs (bullets only)
- `NORMAL`: standard docs
- `DETAILED`: comprehensive docs

Regular speed is `NORMAL`, and is applied when no label is detected.

## Progress Tracking

### PROGRESS_BOARD.md

The `PROGRESS_BOARD.md` file serves as the **single source of truth** for real-time Sprint and Backlog Item status tracking. This file is updated by agents during each phase and provides visibility into the current state of all work.

**Template:**

```Markdown
# Progress board

Progress board is a table showing sprint, and backlog items state. It's the only purpose of this file. All potential comments, progress notes, etc. always keep in dedicated files for each phase.

| Sprint | Sprint Status | Backlog Item | Item Status |
|--------|---------------|--------------|-------------|
| Sprint 1 | implemented | GHC-1 | tested |
| Sprint 2 | implemented | GHC-3 | implemented |
| Sprint 3 | implemented | GHC-4 | tested |
| Sprint 3 | implemented | GHC-5 | tested |
| Sprint 4 | implemented | GHC-6 | implemented |
| Sprint 5 | implemented | GHC-7 | tested |
```

**Purpose:**

- Track Sprint progress through RUP phases
- Monitor individual Backlog Item status
- Provide real-time visibility without reading PLAN.md
- Separate concerns: PLAN.md (high-level plan) vs PROGRESS_BOARD.md (execution tracking)

**Sprint Status Values (Real-Time Tracking):**

- `under_analysis` - Inception phase in progress
- `analysed` - Analysis complete, ready for design
- `under_design` - Elaboration phase in progress
- `designed` - Design complete and approved
- `under_construction` - Construction phase in progress
- `implemented` - All items implemented successfully
- `implemented_partially` - Some items failed or incomplete
- `tested` - All tests passed
- `failed` - Sprint failed to complete

**Backlog Item Status Values (Real-Time Tracking):**

- `under_analysis` - Being analyzed
- `analysed` - Analysis complete
- `under_design` - Design in progress
- `designed` - Design approved
- `test_specified` - Test specs and skeletons written, ready for construction
- `under_construction` - Implementation in progress
- `smoke_passed` - Smoke tests pass; build is testable
- `unit_tested` - All unit tests pass (old + new)
- `integration_tested` - All integration tests pass (old + new)
- `implemented` - Code complete
- `tested` - All quality gates passed
- `failed` - Failed after attempts

**Update Rules:**

- Agents update PROGRESS_BOARD.md during their phase
- Status updates are an **allowed exception** to general editing rules
- Updates happen at phase transitions (start/end of each phase)
- Final statuses set only after all work complete

**Relationship to PLAN.md FSM:**
The PROGRESS_BOARD.md uses granular real-time states, while PLAN.md maintains high-level lifecycle states (Planned → Progress → Designed → Implemented → Tested → Done). Product Owner updates PLAN.md based on PROGRESS_BOARD.md status.

## Cooperation flow

The RUP process follows a 5-phase workflow with test-first quality gates:

### Phase 1: Setup (Contracting + Inception)

1. Review project scope (`BACKLOG.md`) and plan (`PLAN.md`)
2. Review all rules in `rules/generic` and `rules/specific` directories
3. Analyze Backlog Items assigned to Sprint
4. Review previous Sprint artifacts for compatibility
5. Updates PROGRESS_BOARD.md with `under_analysis` status
6. Create combined setup document and commit

**Output:** `progress/sprint_${no}/sprint_${no}_setup.md` (contains Contract + Analysis sections)

### Phase 2: Design + Test Specification

1. Designer Agent reviews analysis from Phase 1
2. Creates detailed technical design for each Backlog Item
3. Performs feasibility analysis against available APIs
4. **Creates Testing Strategy section** (see `rules/generic/testing_strategy_template.md`)
5. Test Architect creates test specifications and skeletons
6. Updates PROGRESS_BOARD.md: `under_design` → `designed` → `test_specified`
7. **YOLO mode:** Self-approve; **Managed mode:** Wait for approval
8. Commits design, test spec, and test skeletons

**Outputs:**

- `progress/sprint_${no}/sprint_${no}_design.md` (includes `## Test Specification`)
- `progress/sprint_${no}/new_tests.manifest`
- Test skeletons in `tests/smoke/`, `tests/unit/`, `tests/integration/`

### Phase 3: Construction

1. Constructor Agent reviews approved design
2. Updates PROGRESS_BOARD.md to `under_construction`
3. Implements code based on design specifications
4. **Fills in test skeletons** (does NOT create new tests)
5. Commits implementation

**Output:** `progress/sprint_${no}/sprint_${no}_implementation.md`

### Phase 4: Quality Gates

1. Test Executor runs quality gates using `tests/run.sh`
2. **Phase A (New-Code):** Run tests from `new_tests.manifest` (A1 smoke → A2 unit → A3 integration)
3. **Phase B (Regression):** Run full suite at specified levels (B1 smoke → B2 unit → B3 integration)
4. On failure: hand report to Constructor, fix, re-run (up to 10 retries)
5. Updates PROGRESS_BOARD.md: `smoke_passed` → `unit_tested` → `integration_tested` → `tested`
6. Commits test logs and results

**Outputs:**

- `progress/sprint_${no}/sprint_${no}_tests.md`
- `progress/sprint_${no}/test_run_*.log` (timestamped logs per gate)

### Phase 5: Wrap-up (Documentation)

1. Documentor Agent validates all Sprint documentation
2. Verifies code snippets are copy-paste-able (no `exit` commands)
3. Creates symbolic links in `progress/backlog/` for traceability
4. Updates `README.md` with recent developments
5. Commits documentation updates

**Outputs:**

- Updated `README.md`
- Symbolic links in `progress/backlog/${BACKLOG_ITEM_ID}/`

## Testing

### Centralized Test Structure

All executable tests live in `tests/` at the repo root:

```
tests/
├── smoke/           # Quick critical checks
├── unit/            # Function-level tests
├── integration/     # End-to-end tests
├── manifests/       # Component test registries
│   └── component_*.manifest
└── run.sh           # Test runner entry point
```

**Principles:**

- One file per component/domain, NOT per sprint
- New test cases are appended to existing files
- `run.sh` is the single entry point (`--smoke`, `--unit`, `--integration`)

### General Testing Requirements

1. Correlation must be tested with parallel executions proving that parallel clients will always have access to workflows triggered by them.

2. Negative test may try to break the link between client call and the actual workflow run

More specific testing may be specified for each `Backlog Item` and `Sprint`.

### Test Documentation Requirements

All test documentation in `progress/sprint_${no}/sprint_${no}_tests.md` MUST comply with:

**Critical Requirements:**

- ✅ All tests MUST be copy-paste-able shell sequences
- ✅ Tests MUST be executable without modification (except tokens/secrets)
- ✅ Expected output MUST be documented
- ✅ Both success and error cases MUST be tested
- ❌ **NEVER use `exit 1` or any exit command in copy/paste examples** (user terminal will close)
- ✅ Prerequisites clearly listed
- ✅ Verification steps provided
- ✅ Test status recorded (PASS/FAIL)
- ✅ Test summary table with results

**Example Structure:**

```markdown
### Test 1: [Test Name]

**Purpose:** [What this test validates]

**Expected Outcome:** [What should happen]

**Test Sequence:**
```bash
# Step 1: [description]
command-to-execute

# Step 2: [description]
another-command

# Expected output:
# [show expected output]

# Verification:
[how to verify success]
```

**Status:** [PASS | FAIL | PENDING]
```

### Implementation Documentation Requirements

All implementation documentation in `progress/sprint_${no}/sprint_${no}_implementation.md` MUST include:

**User Documentation Section:**

- Overview of what was implemented
- Prerequisites clearly listed
- Usage examples (copy-paste-able)
- ❌ **No `exit` commands in examples**
- Expected outputs shown
- Error handling examples
- Options/parameters documented
- Special notes for edge cases

**Example Structure:**

```markdown
#### Usage

**Basic Usage:**
```bash
# Execute the script
./script.sh [options]
```

**Examples:**

Example 1: Normal operation
```bash
# Complete copy-paste example
./script.sh --option value
```

Expected output:
```
[show expected output]
```
```

## Backlog Traceability

To maintain complete requirement traceability from backlog items to implementation, symbolic links are created in the `progress/backlog/` directory structure.

### Purpose

- Complete traceability from requirement to implementation
- Easy navigation: `progress/backlog/GH-15/` shows all GH-15 related documents
- Cross-sprint visibility for multi-sprint backlog items
- Historical audit trail

### Structure

For each Backlog Item processed in a Sprint, create:

```text
progress/backlog/${BACKLOG_ITEM_ID}/
  ├── sprint_${no}_analysis.md -> ../../sprint_${no}/sprint_${no}_analysis.md
  ├── sprint_${no}_design.md -> ../../sprint_${no}/sprint_${no}_design.md
  ├── sprint_${no}_implementation.md -> ../../sprint_${no}/sprint_${no}_implementation.md
  ├── sprint_${no}_tests.md -> ../../sprint_${no}/sprint_${no}_tests.md
  └── sprint_${no}_documentation.md -> ../../sprint_${no}/sprint_${no}_documentation.md
```

### Creation Process

**Step 1:** Identify Backlog Items from `PLAN.md` for current sprint

**Step 2:** Create Backlog Item directory (if doesn't exist)

```bash
mkdir -p progress/backlog/[BACKLOG-ITEM-ID]
```

**Step 3:** Create symbolic links to all sprint documents

```bash
cd progress/backlog/[BACKLOG-ITEM-ID]
ln -sf ../../sprint_${no}/sprint_${no}_analysis.md .
ln -sf ../../sprint_${no}/sprint_${no}_design.md .
ln -sf ../../sprint_${no}/sprint_${no}_implementation.md .
ln -sf ../../sprint_${no}/sprint_${no}_tests.md .
ln -sf ../../sprint_${no}/sprint_${no}_documentation.md .
```

**Step 4:** Verify links work

```bash
ls -la progress/backlog/[BACKLOG-ITEM-ID]/
# Verify all links point to existing files
```

### Example

Sprint 15 with GH-14, GH-15, GH-16:

```bash
mkdir -p progress/backlog/{GH-14,GH-15,GH-16}
cd progress/backlog/GH-14 && ln -sf ../../sprint_15/*.md . && cd ../..
cd progress/backlog/GH-15 && ln -sf ../../sprint_15/*.md . && cd ../..
cd progress/backlog/GH-16 && ln -sf ../../sprint_15/*.md . && cd ../..
```

### Responsibility

The **Documentor Agent** (Phase 5) is responsible for creating and maintaining these symbolic links during the Documentation phase.

## Appendix A. Document rules

### Editing

1. Use Markdown

2. Do not use any indention under chapters. Each paragraph starts always at column zero. Exception are enumerations.

3. Always add an empty line before any code blocks, enumerations. Follow Markdown linting rules.

4. Always add an empty line after chapters, list headers. Follow Markdown linting rules.

### Content ownership

**Document Ownership by Agent:**

| Document | Owner | Editing Rules |
|----------|-------|---------------|
| `PLAN.md` | Product Owner | Read-only for agents |
| `BACKLOG.md` | Product Owner | Read-only for agents |
| `PROGRESS_BOARD.md` | All Agents | Update during respective phases |
| Analysis documents | Analyst Agent | Create and own during Inception |

| Implementation docs | Constructor Agent | Create and own during Construction |
| Test documents | Constructor Agent | Create and own during Construction |
| Documentation summary | Documentor Agent | Create and own during Documentation |
| Proposed changes | Any Agent | Append-only, never edit existing |
| Open questions | Any Agent | Append-only, never edit existing |

**Key Rules:**

1. Any change to completed work or Implementation Plan (`PLAN.md`) goes through `Proposed changes` and `More information needed` process.

2. Never edit documents from other Sprints - only current Sprint documents.

3. Never edit status tokens - these are owned by Product Owner.

4. Design Status lines in phase documents are owned by Product Owner except initial "Proposed" status set by Designer Agent.

5. Agents can only edit documents during their respective phase or as explicitly allowed.

## P4. A sprint may deliver multiple coherent outcomes

A sprint may contain multiple independently coherent backlog items when they share a common iteration objective, have manageable dependencies, and can be reviewed together. This is particularly appropriate for Inception and Elaboration, where one iteration can establish several connected artifacts such as requirements, risks, scope, and an architecture baseline.

Each backlog item must retain its own value statement and acceptance signal. The sprint design and wrap-up must identify the evidence for each item, so grouping does not hide incomplete work or weaken traceability. Split items into separate sprints when their dependencies, risk, approval needs, or validation methods would make a single review unclear.

## P5. Process entry point and local method adoption

The project root `BACKLOG.md` is the source of Product Owner priorities. The project root `PLAN.md` is the source of sprint selection and status. When installed, the root `RUP_patch.md` points to `RUPStrikesBack.patch/RUP_patch.md`, which defines local policy that supplements or overrides the generic method in the `RUPStrikesBack` submodule.

Sprint 0 is marked `Progress` by the bootstrap plan. To execute it, the Product Owner explicitly invokes the Codex `rup-strikes-back` skill in the declared mode. For a later planned sprint, the Product Owner first changes that sprint’s status in the root `PLAN.md` from `Planned` to `Progress`, then explicitly invokes the skill. The agent reads its manager and selected phase procedures from `.agents/skills/rup-strikes-back/references/`, then applies this local patch before executing the sprint.

`rup-strikes-back` is the Codex method entry point. The submodule's `/rup-manager` is a Claude compatibility command, not a native Codex command. Managed mode remains the default: the agent pauses for Product Owner approval at the defined decision points.

## P6. Refine prototype work into hierarchical sub-PBIs

When an accepted Inception architecture identifies a prototype PBI that spans
several independently reviewable pieces of work, the following Elaboration
iteration must refine that parent PBI before prototype construction. This is a
required planning checkpoint, not permission to invent the work during
Inception.

Use hierarchical identifiers in the form `PBI-XX.YY`, where `PBI-XX` is the
accepted parent PBI and `YY` is a sequential child number. For example,
`PBI-011.1`, `PBI-011.2`, and `PBI-011.3` are child work items of `PBI-011`.

Create the child items during the Elaboration sprint's setup/design phase, in
the active sprint's design record. Each child item must state its parent, its
bounded outcome, its acceptance evidence, and its dependency on other child
items. Record the same identifiers on the progress board for status tracking.

Child sub-PBIs are sprint-scoped refinements of their parent, not new
Product-Owner backlog items. Keep the parent PBI in the root `BACKLOG.md` and
`PLAN.md`; promote a child to a new root backlog item only when it gains
independent product value, priority, or deferral authority. In managed mode,
the Product Owner approves the proposed decomposition before prototype
construction starts.

## P7. Read the separate Product Owner preferences file

`RUPStrikesBack.patch/USER_PREFERENCES.md` is this project's plain Markdown
customization file for durable preferences explicitly stated by the Product
Owner. Read it alongside this patch before drafting new or revised
project-authored narrative artifacts or a sprint review. The Product Owner
may amend it through an explicit request; do not infer durable preferences
from incidental conversation. A preference does not change a mandatory
method-defined artifact structure unless the Product Owner explicitly asks
for that process change.

## P8. Reconcile documentation and verify before each commit

# /sprint — Sprint Management

Manage sprints in `PLAN.md`.

## Usage

```
/sprint create [<N>] [--title <title>] [--items <ID1,ID2,...>]
/sprint status [<N>]
/sprint close [<N>]
/sprint start [<N>]
```

## Operations

### create

Create a new sprint entry in `PLAN.md`.

**Steps:**
1. Read `PLAN.md` to find next sprint number (or use provided N)
2. Read `BACKLOG.md` to validate item IDs
3. Ask user for:
   - Title (short description of sprint goal)
   - Mode: `managed` or `YOLO`
   - Test levels: `smoke`, `unit`, `integration`, or `none`
   - Regression levels: `smoke`, `unit`, `integration`, or `none`
   - Backlog items to include (if not provided via --items)
4. Validate all required fields present
5. Append sprint to `PLAN.md`
6. Update `PROGRESS_BOARD.md` — add items with status "Planned"

### status

Show sprint status.

**Steps:**
1. Read `PLAN.md`
2. If N provided, show that sprint; otherwise show active sprint (Status: Progress)
3. Display: status, mode, test/regression requirements, items, progress from PROGRESS_BOARD.md

### start

Start a sprint (transition from Planned to Progress).

**Steps:**
1. Verify sprint exists and has Status: Planned
2. Update sprint status to "Progress" in `PLAN.md`
3. Update `PROGRESS_BOARD.md` — items to "under_analysis"

### close

Complete a sprint.

**Steps:**
1. Verify all quality gates passed (check `progress/sprint_N/sprint_N_tests.md`)
2. Update sprint status to "Done" in `PLAN.md`
3. Update `PROGRESS_BOARD.md` — move items to "Done"
4. Optionally prompt for retrospective notes

---

## Format

See `rules/generic/sprint_definition.md` for full specification.

```markdown
## Sprint <N> - <Title>

Status: Planned | Progress | Done
Mode: managed | YOLO
Test: <smoke | unit | integration | none>
Regression: <smoke | unit | integration | none>

<Optional: 1-2 sentences of context>

Backlog Items:

* <ID>. <Title>
```

## Required Fields

| Field | Values | Default |
|-------|--------|---------|
| Status | `Planned`, `Progress`, `Done` | `Planned` |
| Mode | `managed`, `YOLO` | `managed` |
| Test | `smoke`, `unit`, `integration`, `none` | `unit, integration` |
| Regression | `smoke`, `unit`, `integration`, `none` | `unit, integration` |

## Validation

Before saving, verify:

| Check | Rule |
|-------|------|
| Sprint N | Sequential, no gaps |
| Status | Valid value |
| Mode | Valid value |
| Test | Required, valid values |
| Regression | Required, valid values |
| Items exist | All IDs must exist in BACKLOG.md |
| No duplicates | Item cannot be in multiple active sprints |

## Status Transitions

```
Planned → Progress → Done
                  → Failed
```

- `Planned → Progress`: When `/sprint start` or `/rup-manager` begins
- `Progress → Done`: When `/sprint close` after all gates pass
- `Progress → Failed`: When quality gates fail after retries exhausted

# E.4 — Contract and analysis

## Contract

The Product Owner selected only [PBI-042 and PBI-060](../../BACKLOG.md), excluded
PBI-056 and classified the other suggested additions as Construction work.
On 2026-11-09 the Product Owner accepted and closed E.3 and authorized E.4.
[PLAN](../../PLAN.md) owns assignment/status; [the board](../../PROGRESS_BOARD.md)
owns execution tracking. Managed mode, Test: smoke, integration; Regression:
smoke. This is an Elaboration experiment. External review was completed for the
superseded sequential design. The Product Owner selected independent parallel work
and the announced-release participation flow below, waived another design review,
then approved implementation through handover preparation on 2026-11-09. The
[approved handoff](sprint_E.4_implementation_handoff.md) requires a new dedicated
Astra handover review after implementation and test evidence exist.

The manager, contractor, analyst, designer and test-architecture procedures are
applied with the local patch and Product Owner preferences. The manager's combined
setup record replaces separate contract/analysis summaries. Native SQLcl and
APEX perform capture, staging, release and installation; GitHub provides source
review and visible run evidence. No independent reservation service, private
branch provisioning, production hardening or new test framework is selected.
The explicit approval satisfies the local P8 construction gate. Token usage is not available per phase.

Use GitHub variables/secrets for workflow configuration; generate connections
in RUNNER_TEMP and clean them. Do not create authoritative scratch settings or
expand the prepared-host credential exception. Preserve unrelated working edits.
The review checkpoint may include the existing PBI-060 definition as necessary
review context, without claiming completion or changing its acceptance criterion.

## Analysis

### System boundary and actors

A-01 developers A/B/C independently author and test changes, preserve their feature
branches and choose whether to submit to an announced release. A-02 performs the
Release Manager/integrator responsibility: creates the candidate branch from current
accepted main, announces it, reviews submitted PRs, admits or defers contributions,
and validates the selected combination. A-03 explicitly synchronizes central DEV;
A-04 inspects visible behavior and retained history. A-05 GitHub hosts branches,
release-planning records, PRs and checks. These are responsibilities within the
[SRS actor model](../../docs/srs.md#actors), not additional infrastructure actors.
The bounded journey covers UC-10/7/4/11; it does not complete UC-8/9 onboarding or
FR-8's full atomic reservation contract.

### PBI-060 analysis

Developers work independently in parallel on their feature branches and separate
prepared author fixtures. They do not need a release branch name to begin authoring,
exporting or staging. Each records the accepted main commit from which their own
work started. In the controlled A/B/C demonstration the three start from one common
accepted commit to make independent deltas easy to inspect; this is a fixture choice,
not a rule that constrains when the Release Manager can create a release branch.

Later, the Release Manager creates the next release branch from then-current accepted
main and shares its name with the team. That starting commit can be newer than the
developer starting commits. Git records ancestry; the Release Manager need not locate
or reuse a particular developer's old starting commit. The release baseline is all
accepted content already in main at branch creation, not an empty container for A/C.
The manager records that actual branch-point revision for release provenance.

Developers decide whether their change is ready and whether to join this release.
Those opting in submit a PR whose head is their feature branch and whose base is
the announced release branch. Not submitting to this release is a valid deferral,
not a review failure. The Release Manager then makes a separate admission decision
from source/distribution review, check results and dependencies. A submitted change
can still require correction or be deferred; opting in does not guarantee inclusion.
